# Where to spend the retention budget

To: [PLACEHOLDER: name and role]
From: [PLACEHOLDER: your name]

*Public dataset. Analysis illustrates method, not a real company's results.*

## The problem

26.5% of our 7,043 customers left. They were paying $139,131 a month
between them, which is $1,669,570 a year. We want one way to keep people that pays for itself.

## What I found

Short contracts leave. Month-to-month customers left at 42.7%, against 2.8% on
two-year contracts. They account for 86.9% of the money at risk.

The first year decides it. In the 0-6 months band, 52.9% left. Customers with
12 months or less are 31.0% of the base and 49.6% of the money at risk.

New customers on big bills are the sharpest problem. In the New High-Spend group, under a year with
us and paying a lot, 68.8% left. They're 11.8% of customers and
34.3% of the money at risk.

## What I'd do

Offer New High-Spend customers 15% off for 12 months if they move to a
one-year contract. Test it against a group that gets no offer before rolling it out.

| | Over 12 months |
|---|---:|
| Customers offered | 831 |
| Kept who would have left | 143 |
| Billing kept | $143,319 |
| Cost of the discount | $59,270 |
| Net result | $84,049 |

That assumes 25% of would-be leavers stay because of the offer, and that everyone offered
takes it, including people who were staying anyway. Both numbers are my guesses. It breaks even if
7.8% stay. I gave no extra credit for the longer contract itself. If that helps, it's upside.

Don't put a blanket discount on our biggest group at risk, Established Full Bundle. Most of them stay anyway,
so the same offer there loses $173,121. Look after them instead.

## The risk

The save rate is a guess. If fewer people are persuaded than I assumed, or the offer mostly rewards people
who were staying anyway, the return shrinks. A test over [PLACEHOLDER: test length] measures it before we
commit the budget. All figures are billing, not profit, and they show patterns in the data, not proof that
the offer makes people stay.
